IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01594

What in “Paraclete” Christianity takes the form of a continuing inspiration destined to disclose the hidden meaning of earlier revelations and religions, appears in Shiite language as the meaning, function, and spiritual gift of the Imam. The idea of walâyat goes back to the earliest traditions recorded in the collections of Kolaynî and Saffâr. To speak of walâyat while saying nothing of the Imam’s spiritual gift is more than a paradox: it tears apart what belongs together.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01595

Walâyat is then left hanging in empty space. It cannot be attached to the prophetic mission, for that mission was strictly limited to the tanzîl, the outward communication of Revelation. The initiative of the “return,” the ta’wîl that leads back to its inner meaning, must arise from the very heart of the Muhammadan Reality—from the Imam’s walâyat. That is what walâyat means as Imamate. Did a Sufi master such as Semnâni, every bit as conscious of his Sufism as Haydar Âmolî, consent to tear this unity apart?
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01596

Some scattered statements in his writings seem to suggest that he did. In them, he declares that he chose Sunnism as the “middle way.” His position on the Twelfth Imam, the son of Imam Hasan al-Askarî, is equally explicit.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01597

Like the eleven Imams before him, he considers the Twelfth Imam to have been the spiritual “pole” of his age, during the nineteen years preceding “his death”; the “poles” of Sufism then succeeded him. It is as though the succession of the Imams had passed to the Sufi shaykhs who became the spiritual poles, so that Sufism would indeed be the “true Shiism.” This may well be the conception held by a certain kind of Sufism, but it is easy to see why Shiites reject it so firmly. It cannot be reconciled with their understanding of the Twelfth Imam and the Great Occultation (ghaybat).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01598

For them, the Imam of the present age already exists, having appeared briefly in the past; yet he is also still to come, since his return—his parousia, or final manifestation—is awaited. The Hour of his coming is forever imminent, lending meaning to every present moment, every now. There is another, no less serious difficulty.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01599

In a few lines, Semnâni condemns the “error” of two groups of Shiites. The first supposedly treats Imam Ali as a god, through incarnation (holûl) and a union of divine and human natures (ittihâd). (No Twelver Shiite has ever professed this doctrine. They never tire of insisting that, although the Imams are bearers of the divine Attributes, they remain created beings. Twelver Shiites understand themselves to be following precisely the straight path, sirât mostaqîm, the “middle way” between extremism and Sunnism.) The second group, Semnâni tells us, maintains that prophecy (nobowwat) is the outward aspect of walâyat, and walâyat the inward aspect of prophecy.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01600

Yet to condemn this fundamental teaching of Shiite spiritual knowledge is not merely to put himself at odds with Shiism. It is to put Semnâni at odds with himself—with his entire Tafsîr, and with the very idea of walâyat that enables him, throughout that commentary, to bring the meaning of prophecy into the inner life.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01601
Confronted with these clashing assertions, one’s first reaction is bewilderment.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01602

But it soon becomes clear that we are facing precisely the situation that Haydar Âmolî denounced so forcefully during that same eighth Islamic/fourteenth Christian century. Sayyed Haydar, like Semnâni, embraced the paradox that the Sufis are “the true Shiites.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01603

But he did so while professing Twelver Shiism in its entirety, laying claim to the full tradition of its spiritual knowledge and writing, alongside his Jâmi’ al-asrâr, a monumental Shiite commentary on Ibn Arabî’s Fosûs. What, then, was Semnâni’s secret? We must never forget the importance of ketmân, or taqîyeh: the “discipline of the secret,” prescribed by the Imams and practiced by Shiites over so many centuries.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01604

Shiite esotericism is no empty expression; one may often encounter a Shiite without suspecting it. This discipline meant, on the one hand, respect for a truth that should be given only to those worthy and capable of receiving it, and, on the other, the need to protect oneself against persecution. We may therefore ask to what extent Semnâni himself made use of this protection.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01605

But to stop at that question, whatever the answer, would be to travel only halfway along the spiritual path on which he invites his reader. At the end of that path stands the idea of the latîfa jabrâ’eliya, the “angel Gabriel of your being.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01606

Ultimately this is none other than the invisible master, the ostâd ghaybî, who discloses the hidden meaning of Qur’anic verses to the mystic and thereby makes it possible to discover the entire prophetic tradition within oneself. Perhaps this is where we should seek Semnâni’s secret: a secret of his spiritual teaching that was destined to bear further fruit.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01607
The idea of an invisible master, a personal guide within, is especially alive in the spirituality of Najmoddîn Kobrâ’s school, the spiritual lineage to which Semnâni belongs.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01608

Najm Kobrâ even described in detail how this Figure, this person of light, appears as an imaginal vision to the inner sight (basîra). (The expression shakhs nûrânî, “person of light,” is precisely the one Shiite theosophers use, in the plural ashkhâs nûrânîya, for the Fourteen Immaculate Ones in their existence within the divine fullness.) “It is this person of light before you,” Najm Kobrâ writes, “who is called, in the terminology of Sufism, the Guide of the unseen world (moqaddam al-ghayb). He is also called the personal master of the unseen world (shaykh al-ghayb), or the spiritual Balance of the unseen world (mîzân al-ghayb).”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01609

Still other names are bestowed on him: Guide of Light, like the Sun of the Heart; Sun of Certainty; Sun of Faith; Spiritual Sun of the Spirit. And Najm Kobrâ declares even more explicitly: “Know that the mystic has a witness (shâhid). He is the one called the personal Master in the unseen world. He lifts the mystic toward heaven, and so it is in heaven that he appears.” He is the “Witness in Heaven.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01610

All these names point us back toward the spiritual being whom Suhrawardî, drawing on the Hermetic tradition, called the “Perfect Nature” (see above, Book II, chapter III, §5, and chapter VI, in the discussion of “the angel of the gnostic”).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01611

Equally revealing is the fact that a profound Shiite theosopher such as Qâzî Sa’îd Qommî, in his commentary on Ibn Bâbûyeh’s Tawhîd, identifies the Imam’s function with that of the Angel of the Human Species (rabb al-nû’ al-insânî) in the philosophy of the Master of Illumination, Suhrawardî. This figure of the Perfect Nature had earlier led us back to the Zoroastrian Fravarti, the heavenly archetype and counterpart of a being of light who has come into this world.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01612

Najm Kobrâ says essentially the same thing when he calls the “Witness in Heaven” the mîzân al-ghayb, the “balance,” the counterpart of the earthly self in the spiritual world. Taken together, these facts further strengthen what we have already established about this figure.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01613

All this, then, also lies behind Semnâni’s idea of the ostâd ghaybî, the invisible master and guide. He is indeed the shaykh al-ghayb revealed in Najm Kobrâ’s visions. Just as the visible, outward master teaches tafsîr, the interpretation of the revealed text, so the invisible, inward master discloses ta’wîl, its hidden meaning, to the person who has received spiritual inspiration.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01614

We shall read Semnâni’s text in a few pages; it is extraordinarily rich in suggestion. The inspired mystic stands in relation to his ostâd ghaybî as the Prophet Mohammad stood in relation to the angel Gabriel, the Holy Spirit. This is why the highest latîfa, or subtle organ, is also associated with the “Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary,” where the Prophet saw Gabriel standing in Paradise (53:14).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01615
Hence the preeminence of the color green, which the Prophet saw covering the whole horizon of heaven in his first vision of the Angel.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01616

We can now understand immediately why the ostâd ghaybî is also called the latîfa jabrâ’eliya, the “angel Gabriel of your being.” We might equally say that this inner Gabriel stands in relation to the Angel of Revelation as the Perfect Nature stands in relation to the Angel of the Human Species in Suhrawardî’s Hermetic philosophy.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01617
We can also understand why so many mystics, from Jalâl Rûmî to Mîr Dâmâd, have contemplated the Annunciation of Gabriel, the Holy Spirit, to Mary as a message addressed to every mystic.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01618

There is something more. The Angel who, in the study of prophecy, is the Angel of Revelation, and who, in the “Eastern theosophy” of the Illuminationists (Ishrâqîyûn), is the Angel of Knowledge, appears here as the Angel of ta’wîl, of spiritual interpretation. He reveals the hidden meaning of earlier revelations, provided that the mystic possesses the hearing of the heart, the “heavenly” (malakûtî) sense of hearing.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01619

To this extent, he takes on the spiritual function that belongs to the Imam in Shiism. For by initiating the believer into hidden meaning, the Imam imparts walâyat, which is a spiritual birth for the person who receives it. We may therefore say that Semnâni’s complete inward transformation of the doctrine of prophecy goes hand in hand with an equally complete inward transformation of the doctrine of the Imamate. The Imam becomes the personal, invisible, inward master.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01620

Hence, in Semnâni’s vocabulary, we might call the latîfa jabrâ’eliya—the “angel Gabriel of your being,” who presides over all the other latîfa and reveals the inner meaning of each “prophet of your being”—the “Imam of your being” (Imâm wojûdî-ka). Such a way of experiencing the Imam would be perfectly in tune with the lived devotion of Shiite mystics, the orafâ. I am reminded of a distinguished Shiite shaykh in present-day Iran. A disciple asked him: “Where is the Hidden Imam?” He answered: “Within you, if you can discover him.” One does not say such things from the pulpit or in the public square.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01621

Yet throughout the ghaybat, the Great Occultation, the Imam, as personal guide, is above all—and exclusively—the ostâd ghaybî: the hidden, invisible personal master, whose presence is sometimes disclosed in fleeting appearances, without the person to whom he appears realizing who he is until afterward (see below, Book VII).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01622

We shall therefore leave Semnâni in possession of his secret. Perhaps he sincerely declared himself a Sunni, having chosen Sufism within Sunnism because he believed that the Sufis were “the true Shiites.” Or perhaps he made the declaration in obedience to ketmân, the “discipline of the secret.” In either case, his work can lead a Shiite seeker who knows how to read it all the way to the sanctuary of the Hidden Imam. That sanctuary is not reached through an outward faith, a fides historica, but as one enters a liturgical mystery celebrated in the innermost heart.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01623

We shall regard Semnâni as a great spiritual master, whose surviving works in Arabic and Persian alike ought to be published for their exceptional riches of speculative spiritual philosophy and lived spiritual experience. Even if a Shiite reader sees in his work “a doctrine of the Imamate that dares not speak its name”—because perhaps only someone with Haydar Âmolî’s courage could have given it that name—it remains true that Semnâni, by revealing the seeker’s invisible guide, the “angel Gabriel of his being,” opens the way to the highest organ of the subtle body: the latîfa haqqîya, the “Mohammad of his being.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01624

Only on reaching this summit of the hidden meaning of prophecy, this visio smaragdina, or emerald vision, does one become fully “Muhammadan.” For no one can change the fact that this hidden meaning is what it is: walâyat. Later on (§7), perhaps we shall gain an even deeper sense of what this latîfa, the “angel Gabriel of your being,” signifies. Semnâni writes: “This subtle divine sense of one’s being is, for every seeker, the supreme horizon (al-ofq al-mobîn). The reality of our essential Self (li-anâ’îyati-nâ) cannot pass beyond it (tajâwoz, transgress that horizon).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01625

“And so, whoever reaches this point—whether by traveling the path, walking, flying, or entering ecstasy—whoever brings the powers of all his subtle organs out from the stains of illusion and relativity and allows them to appear as they should appear in their purity: that person, truly, is Muhammadan in the fullest sense. Otherwise, do not deceive yourself. Do not imagine that merely pronouncing the words, ‘I bear witness that Mohammad is the Messenger of God,’ is enough to make you Muhammadan.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
en-book-4-ch-4-s4
4. The Four Modes of Being of the Revealed Book
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01626

Semnâni thus insists with particular force that a faith limited to acknowledging a historical event, and related only to that outward event, is utterly powerless. In Luther’s language, this is fides historica seu mortua: historical, or dead, faith. For faith to have any transforming power, the event must become an inner reality. This requires an organic connection between the method of interpretation that penetrates ever deeper into hidden meanings and the spiritual states that arise within the mystic.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01627

The link between interpretation and mystical anthropology means that understanding of these meanings can advance only as the subtle organism concealed within the human being grows. This subtle body develops “from prophet to prophet,” each prophet representing one of its members or “centers,” until it reaches the Muhammadan organ that supports the Self in which God becomes manifest.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01628

An interpretation grounded in the prophets must therefore correspond to an understanding of the human being grounded in those same prophets. We are about to encounter a structure even more complex than the sevenfold account of inner meaning presented in the short work by the anonymous Iranian author discussed earlier (chapter II). Although that structure could already be related to Semnâni’s seven latîfa, here there is something further.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01629

The seven hidden meanings of the Qur’an do indeed correspond to the seven centers of the subtle organism concealed within the human being. That organism develops as a person comes to understand the hidden meanings proper to each center. Seen in this light, the interpretation of scripture is inseparable from mystical anthropology—an understanding of the human being’s spiritual constitution.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01630

But these hidden meanings also correspond to different modes of being of the Holy Book itself, which in turn correspond to the stages of creation. Here we must return to a profound idea: the cosmic text and the written text of the Book, the creative Word and the Word fixed in writing, are two aspects of one and the same process. Seen in this light, the interpretation of scripture is inseparable from cosmology and cosmogony, from the structure and unfolding of the universe.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01631

To understand the different states of the “eternal Book,” we must therefore turn to Semnâni’s cosmological scheme, which we can only sketch here. For it is this account of creation and the cosmos that ultimately explains how the organs of the subtle body are formed: the substantial influences and cosmic energies that give birth to them and determine their capacity for knowledge. We already know that the seven organs or centers of the subtle body are represented by seven prophets, the “prophets of your inner being.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01632
We can thus begin to glimpse the extraordinary complexity of the doctrine.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01633
The four modes of being of the Book rise in order from the lowest to the highest.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01634
First is its outward state: the Word set down in ink on paper, conveying the literal meaning understood by the overwhelming majority of people.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01635

But this outward form is the body that supports everything else. Even the deepest interpretation of hidden meanings can never dispense with it or abolish it. (This, precisely, is what distinguishes a symbol from an allegory.) Above this outward form, the material appearance of the Book, come three further levels.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01636

Each is represented by a designation of the Book taken from the Qur’an itself, as in the work of our anonymous Sufi discussed earlier (chapter II). Semnâni does not assign precisely the same meanings to these designations, but the difference is of little consequence here. Everything that follows should also be compared with our earlier discussion of the “successive manifestations of the Book” (Book I, chapter V, §2).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01637

Semnâni puts it this way: “Be on your guard. Flee the demonic suggestion that the stories [hikâyât] related in the Qur’an are incoherent accounts. Do not go astray or become one of the condemned. Be certain that anyone who rejects the tafsîr of the Qur’an’s outward meaning (zâhir) in the world of external human events (’âlam al-âfâq al-nâsûtî) is a heretical Bâtini.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01638

“Conversely, anyone who rejects the interpretation—that is, the ta’wîl—of the Qur’an’s inner meaning (bâtin) in the heavenly inner world of the soul (’âlam al-anfos al-malakûtî) is a denier, an enemy of enlightenment, and a fool.” (His terms are severe.) “But whoever brings the outward and inward meanings together—the visible and the hidden—is a true moslim, one of the Chosen. Whoever knows the ‘limit,’ or essential Idea, of the Qur’an in the world of the Jabarût [the world of the divine Attributes and angelic Intelligences] is a mu’min, a true believer, a knower of spiritual realities (’ârif) who follows the Straight Path.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01639

“Finally, whoever knows the summit of the Qur’an’s upward, inward path of interpretation (mottala’) in the world of the Lâhût [the divine realm] is one of the excellent, a Perfect One, a witness before humanity, an initiate into the mysteries, a noble and glorious being.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01640

We are thus shown the Book’s different modes of being—what we might call the “cosmogony of the Book”—and how each corresponds to the spiritual standing of someone able to understand the Book at that “cosmic” level, through the gradual growth of the subtle organs, or latîfa. In practice, we see throughout Semnâni’s Tafsîr that he readily explains the hidden meanings belonging to the “Glorious Book” at the level of the Malakût, where interpretation falls within the domain of walâyat.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01641

But whenever an interpretation would require him to disclose a meaning at the level of the Jabarût or the Lâhût, he draws back, invoking the discipline of the secret, which forbids him to reveal it. The same reserve can be observed in many Shiite authors.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01642

There is a further correspondence. The spiritual standing produced by understanding the Book at a particular level also corresponds to the kind of interpretive authority appropriate to that mode of being. This will show us just how deeply we are within a Shiite sphere of influence. As noted earlier, Semnâni analyzes the matter with great precision. In its ideal and perfect fullness, the Imam’s function has three aspects.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01643

Khilâfat is succession to the outward government of the community: its temporal affairs. Walâyat is the Imam’s status as a “Friend of God,” investing him with the initiatory function of a purely “spiritual priesthood”; in this respect the Imam stands in relation to the Prophet as Aaron stood to Moses. Wasâyat is the status of spiritual heir.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01644

In historical fact, the union of these three aspects was always exceptional. (The other eleven Imams did not in practice exercise the khilâfat.) It was realized uniquely, and with incomparable perfection, in the person of the First Imam, Ali ibn Abî-Tâlib, who was thus Imam in a “threefold” sense (fî’l-marâtib al-thalâtha). In him, the light of spiritual authority (walâyat) prevailed over the other two aspects.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01645

Semnâni’s emphatic affirmation of this is all the more significant from the Shiite point of view because he then allows that this ideal perfection may be united again at the end of time in a child descended from Fâtima: the awaited Imam, or Mahdi in the Shiite understanding. Now, Semnâni specifies that the caliphal function—succession to temporal government—belongs properly to the outward aspect of the Book, the text of religious Law. This is entirely consistent with the way someone devoted to inner meaning should understand the workings of society.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01646

Walâyat, the initiatory function, belongs properly to the inward meaning of the Book (and therefore corresponds to the true moslim). Wasâyat, the status of spiritual heir, belongs properly to the Book’s “limit”—the Book in its essential reality or Idea, as it exists in the world of the Jabarût. Here, then, the Imam’s threefold function is understood in relation to the interpretation of the Book’s hidden meaning.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01647

The three technical terms are used in precisely their Shiite theological sense. This use does not occur, and cannot occur, in the framework of Sunni Islam, where what constitutes the scriptural foundation of Shiism is absent: the affirmation of a hidden spiritual meaning and its corollary, the Imamate. (The Sunni understanding of the Imam is purely secular, social, and temporal; the Shiite understanding is essentially metaphysical and “hieratic,” in the Neoplatonic sense of that word.) When the ideas of the Imam and the Imamate are organically linked to the interpretation of hidden meaning, we are, by that very fact, within the sphere of Shiite influence.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01648

We have already suggested how complex the connections are between what openly belongs to Shiism and what belongs to it more discreetly—connections that still need to be investigated. Semnâni’s case seems particularly revealing.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01649

Be that as it may, we are now in a position to follow the outline of his theory of interpretation up to the point where the spiritual seeker, by realizing the “Mohammad of his being,” realizes what we may call the “Imam of his being.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01650

At the lowest level stands the literal, outward meaning (zâhir), perceived by the physical sense of hearing, the outward hearing (sam’ zâhir). Correspondingly, the tafsîr of this outward meaning belongs to the caliphal function, whose concern is solely temporal succession—the outward level of reality. Its validity depends on properly historical testimony, which confirms what is visible and external. This is why anyone who offers his own interpretation of the Qur’an’s outward meaning without having heard it from an interpreter whose chain of transmission leads back to the Prophet’s Companions risks falsifying most of its statements and misunderstanding the reasons and circumstances that prompted the revelation—the “descent” (nozûl)—of its verses.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01651

If we now survey the structure rising above this lowest level, we see three successive heights. Each is represented by a Qur’anic title that establishes the metaphysical character of the text to be understood. First comes the “Glorious Book” (Qorân majîd), read by those who seek its inner meaning in proportion to the growth of their subtle organs (latîfa). This Glorious Book is inscribed on the “Preserved Tablet.” It is the manifestation, or revealed form, of the “August Book” (Qorân karîm), which is concealed in a hidden Book that only the utterly pure may touch—those whom God has already purified of every trace of the world of coming-to-be and passing-away, through the living streams that nourish their subtle organs. The August Book is itself a manifestation of the “Sublime Book” (Qorân ’azîm), concealed in the divine archetype, the “Mother of the Book.” Immediately above the common outward level, then, we encounter the Glorious Book. This is the Book as understood by those who advance through its seven inward meanings, its seven depths (batn). As inner meaning, it is perceived through inward hearing, through the angelic hearing of the heart (al-sam’ al-bâtin al-malakûtî)—that is, through the subtle organ of the heart, the “Abraham of your being.” This suggests that the Book’s mode of being here is the one it possesses in the world of the Malakût, the realm of angelic souls: the heavenly souls of the spheres and human souls. The organs that perceive it therefore belong to the Malakût and are themselves angelic in nature (malakûtî). Its tafsîr, or rather its ta’wîl, comes under walâyat: in Shiite language, the Imam’s spiritual gift of interpretation. Here, significantly, as we anticipated, this function of the Imam is performed by the “invisible inner master.” Anyone who tried to interpret the Qur’an’s inner meaning without divine inspiration (ilhâm) being given to the subtle organs of his higher consciousness, spirit, and innermost secret (sirr, rûh, and khafî—the Moses, David, and Jesus of his being) would betray and profane the inspirations that flash upon those angelic organs (latâ’if malakûtîya) from the realm of divine lordship (Hazrat al-Robûbîya), coming as sudden illuminations (wârida). Just as a healthy physical sense of hearing is necessary for someone to hear the outward Qur’an and receive its tafsîr from an “outward, visible master” (ostâd shahâdî), so an unimpaired hearing of the heart is necessary for the inspired seeker (molham) to hear the Qur’an’s inner meaning and receive its interpretation—its ta’wîl—from an “invisible master” (ostâd ghaybî). The person whose heavenly hearing of the heart is impaired is one of the deaf to whom the verse refers: “Deaf, mute, blind: they understand nothing” (2:166). Here, then, the “invisible and secret” master who teaches ta’wîl to his disciple does indeed appear as the “Imam of his being.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01652

The “August Book” (Qorân karîm) is the Book at its “limit” (hadd), in its essential Idea or reality (haqîqat), as it exists in the world of the Jabarût—the world of the divine Attributes and cherubic Intelligences. It is perceived through a sense of hearing that itself belongs to the Jabarût (al-sam’ al-jabarûtî), and the interpretation (tafsîr, or ta’wîl) of this metaphysical Book belongs to the status of spiritual heir (wasâyat). Anyone who interpreted its “limit,” or haqîqat, without authorization issuing from the secret Temple, the Kaaba of the divine realm (Ka’bat al-olâhîya), would commit a sacrilege against the higher teachings concerning the divine Attributes. Much may lie behind this restriction: a Shiite or an Ismaili could certainly recognize something of his own tradition in it. And indeed, at certain decisive points in his commentary, we see Semnâni draw back and declare that he is not permitted to reveal the interpretation. The health or integrity of the jabarûtî hearing—the capacity to hear in the cherubic world of the divine Attributes—is required in order to receive this interpretation without the mediation of the three subtle organs that still played a part at the preceding level (sirr, rûh, and khafî). Here it is received through the latîfat al-haqqîya alone, the “Mohammad of your being.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01653

The “Sublime Book” (Qorân ’azîm) is the Book preserved in the archetype, the “Mother of the Book.” It stands at the summit of the upward path of interpretation (mottala’), the “Orient” (matla’) where the Book eternally rises. It is perceived through divine hearing (al-sam’ al-lâhûtî). Anyone who attempted to interpret this “Orient” of the Book by that upward path before receiving authorization through admission to the Sublime Presence (Hazrat ’ozmâ), before attaining supreme purity and penetrating to the innermost depth of the divine subtle organ (latîfa haqîqîya) that nourishes and brings to maturity his true spiritual Self (latîfa anâ’îya), would commit a sacrilege against the metaphysical Realities (haqâ’iq) of the Qur’an. Just as healthy, unimpaired cherubic hearing in the world of the Jabarût made it unnecessary to call upon the three intermediaries still needed at the preceding level, so healthy, unimpaired divine hearing is the power to perceive the Book at its “eternal Orient” and receive its interpretation directly from God, without the mediation of the latîfat al-haqqîya. This means that a seeker who reaches this degree of mystical realization no longer needs the “Mohammad of his being” as an intermediary, for he has become that Mohammad himself. (This refers to the formation of that latîfa at the third degree of its perfection.) In other words, the higher Self, which this subtle organ had been nurturing, is now fully formed. The Self, having become a perfect mirror, is itself the organ in which God becomes manifest—the organ of the theophany—and contemplates that manifestation without an intermediary.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01654

At this final point we can fully appreciate the significance of the “invisible inner master,” whom Semnâni described earlier as the one who grants ta’wîl to the inspired mystic. Having become the “Mohammad of his being,” the mystic now occupies a position exactly corresponding to that assigned by the Illuminationists (Ishrâqîyûn) to the spiritual seeker who, through union with the “Active Intelligence,” the Holy Spirit, is invested as the “Seal of Prophecy.” In the teaching of the Illuminationists, the Active Intelligence—or the Perfect Nature—assumes the role of the “invisible master.” In Semnâni’s teaching, the invisible master assumes the Imam’s role and spiritual gift of interpretation.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01655

Moreover, the very word used to describe him (ghaybî, invisible, hidden) gives him a quality that, in one way or another, associates him with the Hidden Imam, who is in a state of occultation (ghaybat) according to Twelver Shiism. The invisible master fulfills the Imam’s function by inspiring the inner meaning, the ta’wîl, in the “prophets of your being.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01656
Thus we may indeed say that the invisible master is none other than the “Imam of your being,” the “inner Imam,” the “Hidden Imam.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01657

We may therefore conclude that the complete inward transformation of the doctrine of prophecy occurs together with an equally complete inward transformation of the doctrine of the Imamate. This helps us understand the relationship between Sufism and Shiism. The Imam is the invisible, inward master who guides the seeker from one hidden meaning to another (see Book I, chapter VII, §4). Here we meet once more the conception of the Imamate formulated by Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî: “a heavenly and uncreated thing within the human being, which is the Imamate.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01658

But unlike the Illuminationists described in the Dabestân, Mollâ Sadrâ was both a Shiite and an Illuminationist—or, more exactly, a Shiite Illuminationist. His own terminology (in his commentary on Kolaynî) includes explicit references to the “inner Imam” (Imâm dâkhilî, Hojjat bâtina). These various names bring us back to the figure Semnâni sometimes calls outright the “secret personal master,” the invisible inner master, and sometimes evokes indirectly as the latîfa jabrâ’eliya, the “angel Gabriel of your being.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01659

And the circle closes when we return to the Illuminationists’ Active Intelligence or Perfect Nature. All these expressions bear witness to one and the same spiritual experience, one and the same encounter at the threshold of the Unseen. We have observed in another setting that this does not mean casting aside the teaching about prophecy. It means realizing its deepest truth in the very heart of the most undeniable personal experience.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01660

Yet this fulfillment of prophecy through a transcendent interpretation that makes its meaning inwardly real could never take place without the doctrine of the Imamate, which is the key to that interpretation. Sufi inwardness is not the enemy of the Shiite Imamate; whether it knows it or not, it is rather the Imamate’s work. Viewed in this way, these matters seem to come into focus as Haydar Âmolî and Mollâ Sadrâ themselves understood them.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01661

All these indications seem to converge toward a final view that brings together what we have already gathered and developed. We have seen that Semnâni accepts that the threefold perfection of the complete Imamate will one day be repeated, at the end of time, in a descendant of Fâtima. This does not mean, as we have said, that he thereby accepts the Twelver Shiite doctrine, according to which the Twelfth Imam is the son of the Eleventh, Hasan al-Askarî, and believers await not his future birth but his return, his final manifestation as the Mahdi.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01662

Nevertheless, it brings Semnâni’s spirituality into harmony with the Shiite spiritual outlook toward the end of time—and does so through a striking transformation of that very expectation into an inward reality. In Semnâni’s eyes, merely sitting and waiting for the Mahdi to appear is the attitude of an ignorant, lazy, irresponsible person. If the blessing spoken whenever the awaited Imam is mentioned—“May God hasten the joy of his coming”—is to be sincere and effective, that coming must take place each time, here and now, invisibly, within the person who utters it.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01663

Semnâni insists: it is within yourself that you must realize the power of the Guided One who is himself the Guide (al-qowwat al-hâdîya al-mahdîya). For it is also within yourself that the forces of the Antichrist (Dajjâl) are present, and it is these forces that the manifestation of the “Mahdi of your being” must drive back and dispel.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01664

We have thus reached the complete inward realization of a Shiism whose presence can hardly be missed wherever the hidden meaning of scripture is interpreted. Perhaps its secret and its surest triumph lie precisely here: in an inward realization that brings Shiism itself to fulfillment at the end of the stages of inward understanding into which it initiates the seeker.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01665

The person who reaches this degree unites within himself the light of the Imamate and the light of prophecy: the light of his “invisible guide” and that of the “Mohammad of his being.” His Self, in which God becomes manifest, takes on the quality of “beloved of God.” It becomes a pure mirror of the divine, and the divine presence moves and animates the Image of itself contemplated in that mirror.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01666
We have surely reached the essential point, and this first outline has given us a glimpse of the supreme goal toward which Semnâni’s method of interpretation seeks to lead us.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01667

Yet even after setting out the main lines that connect the seven subtle organs of the human being with the hierarchy of the Qur’an’s “cosmic” modes of being, many technical details remain to be worked out. In particular, we must account for the actual multiplicity of hidden meanings through which a complete spiritual education must lead the mystic before the goal is reached. The complexity only increases.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01668

Each of the seven centers or organs of the subtle body is itself made up of ten subtle coverings, or latîfa, corresponding to the ten latîfa that develop within the physical organism through the stages of its growth and perfection. Each of these latîfa has its own way of judging and understanding the Book.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01669

We must therefore reckon not simply with seven hidden meanings corresponding to the seven subtle organs, but with seventy. (Seventy is, moreover, a known variant of the number in the celebrated tradition concerning the seven hidden meanings.) And there is a still more distant prospect: each of these subtle coverings or layers, marking a stage in the growth of the original seed, can itself be regarded as possessing ten organs of outward and inward perception, whether potentially or actually.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01670

Thus, in the end, the possibility of seven hundred hidden meanings comes into view. We may be forgiven for feeling dizzy at the thought. Even a master of spiritual experience such as Semnâni can be forgiven for shrinking from the task of carrying out the entire plan. “For my part,” he says, “I have dug down to the water and opened a passage for those who are gifted.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01671

“Now it is for you, O seeker, to descend to the waters of these Mysteries, so that you may deserve the stream flowing from each of the seven subtle centers. Let your outward being be purified by the water of the wisdoms which, descending from the divine Presence, run through the streams of the Qur’anic verses. Renounce the intoxications produced by outward, visible forms, so that you may become capable of intimate converse (monâjât).” By way of experiment and example, Semnâni undertook to give a sevenfold ta’wîl of one verse among many.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01672
We cannot even offer an analysis of this extensive lesson here: it would need to be set out in a comparative table, with the interpretations of the seven meanings advancing in parallel.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01673
Yet it is enough to give us a sense of the ideal task as he conceived it—a task that would have produced a monumental work unlike any other.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01674

The verse chosen for this exercise in interpretation is identified as verse 4 of surah XLVI: “O you who believe, do not approach the Prayer while you are intoxicated; wait until you understand what you are reciting. Nor approach it when you have incurred an impurity other than those one incurs in passing, until you have performed your ablutions.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01675

The verse is perceived and understood, contemplated and fully drawn out in turn at the level of each of the seven subtle centers, through the organ of perception belonging to that center. At every stage, the effort is directed toward bringing about in that center the state that will enable the mystic to move to a higher or deeper degree and to draw nearer to the person of his true Self, leaving behind the illusory self of the bodily soul.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01676

Each time, the people to whom the command is addressed are different: they are the faculties belonging to that subtle center, the “people” of the “prophet” whom the center represents within the world of the soul. Each time, the Prayer that must not be approached in a state of intoxication corresponds to a different degree or form of the divine Presence.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01677

Each time, intoxication—the unconsciousness and ignorance from which these “people” must awaken—brings different dangers, ever more hidden and subtle. Each time, the impurity one might incur is different; but the command remains the same: pass only through the sanctuary (masjad) of each subtle center. For then, however unavoidable contact with appearances may be for those merely passing through, the forms that appear according to the properties of each organ can no longer halt the ascent.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01678

In short, the aim is to escape the danger of what we earlier called a failed initiation, to prevent the illness that makes the “angelic hearing of the heart,” the organs of inward hearing, go deaf. To this end, Semnâni lays out various forms of dhikr, the remembrance of God, ascending through seven degrees from ritual dhikr (rasmî) to the supreme dhikr (a’zam).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01679
It is impossible to mistake what is meant here: these are neither allegories nor edifying metaphors.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01680

What is at stake is attaining a way of understanding that, each time, brings a particular way of being into existence. Interpretation and mystical anthropology are inseparable—a point Semnânî insists on emphatically. This is a truth that must be lived: whichever subtle center, or latîfa, one reaches and inhabits, one becomes the human being proper to that latîfa.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01681

Every way of understanding reveals an inner spiritual state. In examining these states, mystical anthropology naturally arrives at the categories of Gnostic anthropology: those of the first latîfa are the material, or hylic, human beings; those of the second are the psychic, or soul-centered, human beings; and those of the remaining five are the pneumatic, or spiritual, human beings at successive stages of their development.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01682

At each stage, the faculties belonging to that latîfa form, as it were, its own “peoples.” They enjoy all the delights appropriate to its maturity and health, or suffer the disasters that follow its decline, when it can no longer lead the “pilgrim” onward into the latîfa above it. Of course our shaykh knows what his claims demand: “No one will believe what I have just said until he has himself traveled the mystical Way, and has seen with a vision belonging to his own eyes the things that my explanations have enabled him to hear about.”
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
en-book-4-ch-4-s5
5. The Three Bodies of the Human Being
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01683

Because these are not allegories but something real and substantial that must be brought into being, the interpretation of meaning at its seven depths translates directly into mystical anthropology. We have seen Semnânî describe the “subtle center of the heart” as the “Abraham of your being,” because it holds the pearl of a spiritual offspring that the mystic must bring to birth. This child is the true Self in its divine reality: the theophanic Self, capable of reflecting the divine Face.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01684

Yet the child can grow only if it is surrounded and protected by a subtle membrane to whose formation all the latîfa contribute. This protective envelope is the body of spiritual fruition: the subtle body acquired (jism moktasab) through spiritual practice. Semnânî returns repeatedly to this imperishable, acquired subtle body, sometimes in direct teaching, sometimes through a symbol—the microcosmic egg. The theme stands at the heart of his account of the cosmos and the soul.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01685

Indeed, it provides the point of connection, the transition, at which his cosmology joins his prophetic psychology: the point where the latter's seven latîfa meet the cosmic influences or energies of which they are formed.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01686

The human being has three bodies: (a) the original body, the perishable earthly body studied by biology (jism maj’ûl, donyâwî); (b) the acquired body, or body of spiritual fruition (jism moktasab), which is imperishable and corresponds to some extent to the Neoplatonists' okhêma, the soul's subtle vehicle, and which belongs to mystical anthropology; and (c) the resurrection body, literally the “gathered body” (jism mahshûr), assembled on the day of the Great Resurrection (Qiyâmat kobrâ).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01687

Our shaykh likes to point out that a similar power of attraction forms each of these three bodies. The original material particle placed in Adam's loins—that is, in the human being—draws to itself every kindred particle of the element Earth, until the physical organism reaches its full growth and becomes the protective casing, or womb, of the acquired body.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01688

In the same way, an influence proceeding both from the universal Soul and from the individual soul that governs the physical body draws to itself, by a law of affinity, all the subtle substances belonging to the world of the divine Command (’âlam al-Amr), the world of creative creation. These are the latâ’if amrîya, the subtle substances that enter into the formation of the subtle organs. Even when dispersed or hidden in the world of the Elements (’âlam al-khalq, the world of created creation), the soul draws them together into an enduring subtle body that will forever envelop the true spiritual Self.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01689

Finally, on the day of the Great Resurrection, the Rûh, the Spirit, will attract and gather the scattered atoms of the vanished physical body. This “gathered body” will become the eternal garment of the “body of fruition,” just as the latter is already the subtle and imperishable garment of the subtle substance of the true Self (latîfat al-anâ’îya).
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01690

In short, whatever is imperishable and inseparable from the soul's influence is the spiritual or acquired body. Whatever is imperishable yet becomes separated from the soul after the physical organism has perished, and is destined one day to be gathered again by the divine Command through the Spirit's attractive power on the “plain of Judgment,” is the resurrection body, or “gathered body.” A detailed comparison is needed here with the physics—or rather, the alchemy—of the resurrection body as taught by the Shaykhî school (see below, Book VI). I have discussed it at length elsewhere.
IV. The Seven Subtle Organs of the Human Being According to 'Ala al-Dawla Semnani (d. 1336)
passage-en-01691

Semnânî explains his teaching through comparisons. “If someone,” he says, “objects that a human being is one individual, and so cannot have these three bodies, let him look at an almond and its three coverings (qoshîr). He will learn that the kernel (labb) reaches perfection only within and through those three coverings—so much so that damage to the outer covering causes a defect even in the kernel.
